chicken-lime-rice-soup-mexican:
1. Equipment: a large pot with a lid (6 to 8 quarts), a small pot for the grain, a cutting board, a knife, a ladle, a meat thermometer and 5 containers.
2. Cook your protein first so it can rest while the soup simmers: pat it dry, season it with salt, pepper and 1 tsp ground cumin, and cook it in a hot pan with a little oil over medium-high, 5 to 7 minutes a side, until it reads 165F in the thickest part. Rest it 5 minutes so the juices settle back into the meat, then shred it with two forks.
3. Cook your grain in the small pot: rinse it, then simmer it covered in salted water until tender and the water is absorbed (white rice takes about 18 minutes in 1 1/2 cups of water per cup; brown rice 40 to 45 minutes in 2 cups per cup). Rest it 5 minutes off the heat and fluff it. Weigh it cooked.
4. Dice the onion and your vegetables into even 1/2-inch pieces so they cook at the same rate.
5. Bring the broth to a simmer in the large pot with the onion, 1 tsp dried oregano and a pinch of salt. Add your vegetables and simmer 8 to 10 minutes, until just tender; they soften a little more every time you reheat.
6. Stir the shredded meat and the cooked grain into the pot and simmer 2 minutes, just to heat through. Taste it and add salt if it is flat.
7. Ladle the soup evenly into the 5 containers straight away: a full pot cools too slowly and sits for hours in the 40 to 140F range where bacteria grow fastest.
8. Cool the containers with the lids off until they stop steaming, about 20 to 30 minutes, then seal them, write the date on each, and get them in the fridge within 2 hours of cooking.
9. Keep the avocado and the lime out of the containers: cut avocado browns, and lime juice turns the grain mushy overnight.
10. Storage: fridge 4 days, or freezer 3 months without the avocado.
11. Reheat: microwave 2 to 3 minutes, stirring halfway, or warm it on the stove, with a splash of water if the grain has soaked up the broth. Add the diced avocado, a big squeeze of lime, cilantro and chili flakes to the bowl.
trout-lentil-beet-salad:
1. Equipment: a sheet pan, parchment, a small pot, a bowl, a whisk, a jar for the dressing, and 4 containers.
2. Cook your protein: if it is the canned salmon, drain it well and flake it with a fork, and skip the oven. If it is the trout, pat it dry, season it with salt and pepper, roast it on the lined sheet pan at 400F, 10 to 12 minutes, until it reads 145F and flakes easily, then cool it 10 minutes and lift the flesh off the skin in large flakes.
3. Cook the lentils: rinse them (no soaking needed) and simmer them in 3 cups of water per cup of lentils, 18 to 25 minutes, until tender but still holding their shape. Drain them and spread them on a plate to cool, because hot lentils soak up the dressing and turn to mush.
4. Cook the beets: wrap them in foil and roast them at 400F, 45 to 60 minutes, until a knife slides in with no resistance. Cool them, rub the skins off with a paper towel, and dice them into 1/2-inch pieces.
5. If your fat is the walnuts, toast them in a dry pan over medium, 3 to 4 minutes, until they smell nutty, then chop them roughly, because toasting is what makes them taste like something.
6. Make the dressing: whisk the mustard with 2 tbsp red wine vinegar, a pinch of salt and black pepper. It should taste sharp, because the lentils and beets are sweet and earthy.
7. Toss the lentils and the beets with half the dressing while the lentils are still slightly warm so they drink it in.
8. Divide the lentil and beet mix between the 4 containers, top each with its share of the flaked fish, and finish each container with its share of your fat.
9. Keep the arugula and the rest of the dressing in separate small containers or bags, one per serving, so the greens stay crisp until you eat.
10. Cool everything to room temperature with the lids off, then seal, write the date on each, and refrigerate within 2 hours.
11. Storage: fridge 3 days; cooked fish fades first, so this is a cook-twice-a-week dish. Do not freeze it, because the beets and greens turn watery.
12. To eat: no reheating. Pile the arugula into a bowl, tip the lentils, beets and fish on top, and drizzle on the saved dressing with a grind of black pepper.
everything-eggs-cherry-tomatoes:
1. Equipment: a medium pot with a lid, a bowl of ice water, a slotted spoon, 5 containers and 5 small cups or bags for the seasoning.
2. Set the eggs in the pot in one layer and cover them with cold water by an inch. Starting them in cold water means the shells crack less.
3. Bring the water to a full boil, then cover the pot, take it off the heat and leave it 11 to 12 minutes. The gentle heat sets the yolks firm (160F) without the grey ring a hard boil leaves.
4. Move the eggs to the ice water for 10 minutes. The cold shock stops the cooking and pulls the white away from the shell so they peel clean.
5. Peel them under a trickle of running water, starting at the wide end where the air pocket is.
6. Cut your vegetables into bite-size pieces and pat the pieces dry so they do not sit in their own water.
7. Pack the eggs whole with a serving of your vegetables into each of the 5 containers. Whole eggs keep longer than halved ones, which dry out at the cut.
8. Put a pinch of everything bagel seasoning into each small cup. Salt pulls water out of tomatoes and cucumber within an hour, so it goes on when you eat, never in the container.
9. Everything is already cool from the ice bath, so seal the containers, write the date on each, and refrigerate.
10. Storage: fridge 5 days for peeled eggs in a sealed container; the vegetables are at their best within 3. Do not freeze.
11. To eat: cold, straight from the container. Halve the eggs, drizzle a teaspoon of olive oil over everything, and shower on the seasoning and black pepper.
